She was so caught up in admiring those soft blue eyes, in talking and listening, and in making plans in between, that the evening passed much faster than usual. Supper, which always ended these kinds of gatherings, was already set out and brought closer to the fire before she realized it. With more enthusiasm than usual—though she was never indifferent to doing things properly and with care—she took charge of the meal, helping and encouraging everyone to try the minced chicken and scalloped oysters. She did this with a warmth that she knew would be appreciated by the early-to-bed habits and polite manners of their guests.

Poor Mr. Woodhouse was always torn on these occasions. He liked to have a table set, as it was the way things were done in his youth, but he also believed that supper was unhealthy. So while he welcomed his guests to eat, he was also upset that they would. The only thing he could recommend with complete confidence was a small bowl of thin gruel like his own. Still, he might manage to say something like:

"Mrs. Bates, would you try one of these eggs? A soft-boiled egg isn't bad for you. Serle knows how to boil eggs better than anyone. I wouldn't recommend an egg boiled by anyone else, but you don't have to worry—they're small, you see. One of our little eggs won't hurt you. Miss Bates, let Emma help you with a tiny piece of tart—a very tiny piece. They're all apple tarts. You don't need to worry about bad preserves here. I wouldn't suggest the custard. Mrs. Goddard, would you like half a glass of wine? A small half-glass, mixed into a tumbler of water? I don't think it would upset you."

Emma let her father talk, but she served her guests in a much more satisfying way. On this evening, she especially enjoyed seeing them leave happy. Miss Smith was just as happy as Emma had hoped. Miss Woodhouse was such an important person in Highbury that the idea of being introduced had made her both nervous and excited. But the modest, grateful girl left with a very happy heart, delighted by how kindly Miss Woodhouse had treated her all evening and even shook her hand at the end!

He cursed at me, swung at me, but missed so badly he almost fell over. Then he ran into the fog, tripping twice, and disappeared.

'It's the young man!' I thought, my heart pounding as I recognized him. I imagine I would have felt pain in my liver too, if I had known where it was.

'I'll eat my breakfast before they kill me,' he said. 'I'd do that even if I was going to be hanged on that gallows over there right after. I'll beat the shivers, I bet you.'

When evaluating an author's worth and determining their place among the literary pantheon, we are justified in assessing them from our own perspective and according to our own criteria. Yet, when considering the strength of their work, we must take into account their original intent and compare their creations to the vision they themselves set forth, measuring how much falls short. We differ from Mr. Poe in our views on the aims of art. He believes the goal is the creation of Beauty, and it may be only in the interpretation of that term that we find ourselves at odds. In our remarks on his writings, however, we shall follow his own standard as our guide. The sanctuary of the muse is open from every direction, and there is ample space within it for all who offer tribute or seek prophecy.

In his stories, Mr. Poe has chosen to demonstrate his talent primarily in that shadowy realm that lies at the edge of the plausible and stretches into the strange boundaries of superstition and the unreal. He possesses a striking ability to blend two faculties rarely found together: the capacity to affect the reader's mind with the subtle suggestions of mystery and an attention to detail so thorough that not even a pin or a button escapes notice. Both traits stem naturally from the dominant feature of his intellect, which we have previously mentioned—analysis. This is what sets the artist apart. His mind immediately grasps the desired effect. Once he has decided to evoke certain feelings in the reader, he ensures that every element contributes precisely to the central aim. Even his mystery is calculated in his mind. To him, X is a known variable throughout. In any scene he creates, he understands the chemical nature of all his colors. Although some of his figures may appear indistinct, and the shadows formless, to him the contours are as clear and defined as those of a geometric figure. For this reason, Mr. Poe has no affinity for Mysticism. The Mystic lives within the mystery, is wrapped in it; it tinges all his thoughts; it especially affects his vision, and the most ordinary things acquire a prismatic glow from it. Mr. Poe, by contrast, is an observer from the outside. He examines, he dissects, he watches

“with an eye serene,
The very pulse of the machine,”

for it is essentially a machine to him, with gears and cogs and piston-rods, all working to achieve a specific outcome.

This analytical nature of his mind tempers the poetic, and by giving him the endurance to be meticulous, allows him to inject a remarkable sense of reality into his most fantastical ideas. A monomania he portrays with great strength. He enjoys dissecting one of these mental tumors and tracing all the delicate extensions of its roots. In conjuring images of horror, too, he achieves unusual success, sometimes conveying to us by a faint suggestion some dreadful uncertainty, which is the essence of all horror. He leaves the imagination the task of completing the picture, a task to which only it is suited.

“For much imaginary work was there;
Conceit deceitful, so compact, so kind,
That for Achilles’ image stood his spear
Grasped in an armed hand; himself behind
Was left unseen, save to the eye of mind.”

But when we try to understand how strong their writing is, we should consider what they were trying to achieve. We should compare their work to their own goals and see how close they came. We don’t agree with Mr. Poe about what art should be. He believes the main goal of art is to create beauty, and maybe we only disagree on what beauty means. But when we talk about his writing, we’ll use his own standards. The temple of the god of poetry is open to everyone, and there’s plenty of space for all who come with offerings or seek answers.

In his stories, Mr. Poe shows his talent mainly in the strange area between what is possible and the strange world of superstition and fantasy. He has a rare ability to combine two skills that are not often found together: the power to create mystery that affects the reader’s mind and a careful attention to detail that notices even the smallest things. Both of these come from the main feature of his mind, which we’ve already mentioned: analysis. This is what makes him a true artist. His mind quickly moves toward the effect he wants to create. Once he decides what emotions he wants the reader to feel, he makes sure every part of the story supports that goal. Even his mystery is carefully planned in his mind. To him, everything is clear and known. In any picture he paints, he understands the properties of all his colors. Even if some of his images seem unclear or shadowy, to him the outlines are as clear as a math diagram. Because of this, Mr. Poe doesn’t share the same feelings as the Mystic. The Mystic lives in mystery, is surrounded by it; it influences all his thoughts; it especially affects his vision, and ordinary things seem to have a colorful edge. Mr. Poe, on the other hand, is an observer from the outside. He analyzes, he examines, he watches

“with an eye serene,

because to him, it really is like a machine with wheels and gears and rods, all working together to create a specific result.

These brief and spontaneous letters clearly show that Mr. Poe had the qualities that some people say he didn't—humility, determination, trust in others' friendship, and the ability to be warm and grateful. Our first knowledge of Mr. Poe's move to this city was when we received a visit from a lady who introduced herself as the mother of his wife. The lady's face, made beautiful and holy by her evident self-sacrifice to hardship and tender sorrow, her gentle and sorrowful voice pleading her case, her long-forgotten but habitual and unconscious refined manners, and her respectful and appreciative mention of her son's abilities and claims, showed us at once the presence of one of those angels on earth that women in adversity can be. 'April 5th. I saw the unusual sight of the sun rising while most of the visible world was still in darkness. Eventually, the light spread, and I could see the ice line to the north again. 'April 6th. I was surprised to find the ice edge close by, with a huge stretch of ice going all the way to the horizon in the north. 'April 7th. I got up early and, to my delight, finally saw what I could only think was the North Pole itself. It was there, without a doubt, right beneath me. But alas, I had risen so high that I couldn't see anything clearly. Looking at the numbers showing my altitude between 6 A.M. on April 2nd and 8:40 A.M. the same day (when the barometer dropped), it seemed the balloon had reached at least 7,254 miles above sea level by 4 A.M. on April 7th. In any case, I definitely saw the whole of the Earth's longest diameter; the entire northern half lay beneath me like a map. The equator formed the edge of my view. This is, in fact, the case. I have a lot—very much—that I would be happy to share. I have a great deal to say about the planet’s climate; about its amazing shifts between heat and cold, with scorching sunshine for two weeks straight and then more than polar-like cold the next; about the constant movement of moisture, like distillation in a vacuum, from the side facing the sun to the side facing away; about a shifting zone of liquid water; about the people themselves; about their customs, traditions, and political systems; about their unique physical structure; about their ugliness; about their lack of ears, which are useless in such an atmosphere; about their ignorance of speech and its properties because of that; about their alternative method of communication; and about the strange connection between each person on the moon and a specific person on Earth—a connection similar to and based on the relationship between the planet and its satellites, through which the lives and fates of the moon’s inhabitants are intertwined with those of Earth’s. Upon arriving at the hut, I knocked as was my habit, and receiving no answer, I searched for the key in the spot I knew it was hidden, unlocked the door, and stepped inside. A pleasant fire was burning in the fireplace. It was a welcome sight, and I was glad to see it. I removed my coat, took a chair by the crackling logs, and waited calmly for my hosts to arrive.

Soon after nightfall they came, greeting me with great warmth. Jupiter, beaming with delight, bustled around preparing some marsh hens for supper. Legrand was in one of his fits—how else can I describe them?—of excitement. He had discovered an unfamiliar bivalve, which he believed formed a new genus, and more than that, he had tracked down and captured, with Jupiter’s help, a _scarabæus_ that he thought might be entirely new, though he wanted my opinion on the matter the next day.

“And why not tonight?” I asked, rubbing my hands by the fire, wishing the whole tribe of _scarabæi_ were far away.

“Ah, if only I had known you were here!” Legrand replied. “It’s been so long since I last saw you, and how could I have imagined you would visit on this very night of all nights? On my way home I met Lieutenant G—— from the fort, and, foolishly, I lent him the bug. So you won’t be able to see it until morning. Stay here tonight, and I’ll send Jup to fetch it at sunrise. It is the most beautiful thing in existence!”

“What?—sunrise?”

“Nonsense! No!—the bug. It is a brilliant gold color—about the size of a large hickory-nut—with two jet black spots near one end of the back, and another, a bit longer, at the other. The _antennæ_ are—”

“Dey ain’t no tin in him, Massa Will, I keep a tellin on you,” Jupiter interjected. “De bug is a goole bug, solid, ebery bit of him, inside and all, sep him wing—neber feel half so hebby a bug in my life.”

“Well, suppose it is, Jup,” Legrand replied, with more urgency than the situation seemed to require, “is that any reason for you to let the birds burn? The color”—he turned to me—“is really almost enough to support Jupiter’s idea. You have never seen a more brilliant metallic sheen than the scales emit—but you cannot judge that until tomorrow. In the meantime, I can give you some idea of the shape.” With that, he sat down at a small table where a pen and ink were placed, but there was no paper. He searched a drawer for some, but found none.

“Never mind,” he said at last, “this will do.” And from his waistcoat pocket he pulled out a scrap of what I assumed to be very dirty foolscap, and sketched a rough drawing with the pen. While he did this, I remained seated by the fire, still feeling the chill. When the sketch was finished, he handed it to me without getting up. As I took it, a loud growl was heard, followed by scratching at the door. Jupiter opened it, and a large Newfoundland belonging to Legrand came in, leaping onto my shoulders and showering me with affection; for I had shown him much attention during my previous visits.

When we arrived at the dock, I observed a scythe and three spades, all brand new, resting at the bottom of the boat we were to use.

“What is the purpose of these, Jup?” I asked.

“Him syfe, massa, and spade.”

“Indeed; but why are they here?”

“Him de syfe and de spade what Massa Will told me to buy for him in town, and it cost me a fortune to get ’em.”

“But what, in the name of all that is strange, is your ‘Massa Will’ going to do with scythes and spades?”

“That’s more than I know, and the devil take me if I don’t think it’s more than he knows too. But it’s all because of that bug.”

Since I could gain no clarity from Jupiter, whose mind seemed entirely consumed by 'de bug,' I stepped into the boat and we set sail. With a brisk wind at our backs, we quickly reached the small cove north of Fort Moultrie, and a two-mile walk brought us to the hut. It was about three in the afternoon when we arrived. Legrand had been waiting for us with great anticipation. He seized my hand with a nervous eagerness that unsettled me and reinforced my suspicions. His face was pale, almost deathly so, and his deep-set eyes gleamed with an unnatural brightness. After a few inquiries about his health, I asked him, not knowing what else to say, if he had yet obtained the _scarabæus_ from Lieutenant G——.

“Oh, yes,” he replied, his face flushing, “I got it from him the next morning. Nothing would tempt me to part with that _scarabæus_. Do you know that Jupiter is quite right about it?”

“In what way?” I asked, with a growing sense of unease.

“In thinking it is a bug made of _real gold_.” He spoke with such solemnity that I felt a deep sense of shock.

“This bug is going to make my fortune,” he continued, with a triumphant grin, “to restore me to my family’s estate. Is it any wonder, then, that I value it? Since Fortune has seen fit to give it to me, I only need to use it properly and I shall find the gold it points to. Jupiter; bring me that _scarabæus!_”

“What! de bug, massa? I’d rather not go fetch that bug for you—you must get him for yourself.” Legrand then rose with a solemn and dignified manner and retrieved the beetle from a glass case where it was kept. It was a beautiful scarabæus, and, at that time, unknown to naturalists—naturally a great treasure from a scientific standpoint. There were two round, black spots near one end of its back, and a long one near the other. The scales were incredibly hard and shiny, with the look of polished gold. The weight of the insect was remarkable, and, considering all these things, I could hardly fault Jupiter for his belief about it; but what to make of Legrand’s agreement with that belief, I could not, for the life of me, understand.

This thought made me wonder if there was some meaning or connection to the skull symbol. I also noticed the shape of the parchment. These colors fade after a while when the paper cools down, but they appear again when heat is applied.

The thinking abilities we call analytical are hard to break down. We understand them only by how they work. We know that for someone who has them in great amounts, they bring great joy. Just as a strong person takes pride in their strength and enjoys physical challenges, someone with strong analytical skills takes pride in solving problems. They enjoy even small tasks that let them use their skills. They like puzzles, riddles, and symbols, and they solve them with a sharpness that seems almost magical. Her forehead was clear and wide, her blue eyes bright and clear, and her lips and face showed such sensitivity and sweetness that no one could look at her without thinking she was a special being, almost sent from heaven.

The peasant woman, noticing that my mother was looking at this lovely girl with wonder and admiration, eagerly told her the girl's story. She wasn't her own child, but the daughter of a nobleman from Milan. Her mother was German and had died giving birth to her. The baby had been left with these people to be raised, and they had been better off back then. They had not been married long, and their oldest child had just been born. The father of the girl was one of those Italians who remembered the ancient glory of their country and tried to win back their freedom. He became a victim of his country's weakness. It wasn't known if he had died or was still in Austrian prisons. His property was taken away, and his child became an orphan and a beggar. She stayed with her foster parents and grew up in their simple home, more beautiful than a garden rose among dark-leaved brambles.

When my father returned from Milan, he found a child playing with me in the hall of our villa who was more beautiful than any painted angel—a child who seemed to shine with light from her looks and who moved more lightly than the mountain goats.

So much has been achieved, cried the spirit of Frankenstein—yet I shall accomplish far more; following the path already laid, I will carve a new route, uncover hidden forces, and reveal to the world the deepest secrets of creation.

I did not close my eyes that night. My inner self was in a state of rebellion and unrest; I sensed that order would emerge from it, but I lacked the strength to bring it about. As the morning light broke, sleep finally arrived. I awoke, and the thoughts of the previous night seemed like a dream. Only a determination remained to return to my former studies and to commit myself to a science for which I believed I had a natural gift. On the same day, I visited M. Waldman. His manner in private was even more gentle and appealing than in public, for during his lecture there had been a certain dignity in his bearing that in his own home gave way to the utmost warmth and kindness. I gave him nearly the same account of my past studies as I had given to his fellow professor. He listened attentively to my brief account of my pursuits and smiled at the names of Cornelius Agrippa and Paracelsus, but without the disdain that M. Krempe had shown. He remarked that 'These were individuals whose tireless zeal modern philosophers owed much of their knowledge to. They had left us with the simpler task of assigning new names and organizing the facts they had largely uncovered. The efforts of men of genius, however misguided, rarely fail to eventually benefit mankind.' I listened to his statement, delivered without any arrogance or pretense, and then added that his lecture had dispelled my doubts about modern chemists; I spoke in measured words, with the humility and respect fitting for a young student toward his teacher, without revealing (inexperience would have made me embarrassed) the excitement that drove my future work. I asked for his advice regarding the books I should acquire.

'I am pleased,' said M. Waldman, 'to have found a student; and if your dedication matches your talent, I have no doubt of your success. Chemistry is the field of natural philosophy where the greatest progress has been and can be made; it is for this reason that I have chosen it as my special study; yet at the same time, I have not ignored the other areas of science. A man would make a poor chemist if he focused solely on that one field of human knowledge. If your aim is to truly become a man of science and not merely a minor experimenter, I should advise you to study every branch of natural philosophy, including mathematics.'

He then led me into his laboratory and explained the functions of his various instruments, telling me what I should obtain and promising me the use of his own once I had advanced sufficiently in the science not to disrupt their workings. He also provided me with the list of books I had requested, and I took my leave.

Not much has changed since you left, except for the growth of our dear children. The blue lake and snow-covered mountains never change, and I believe our peaceful home and happy hearts follow the same unchanging rules. My small tasks keep me busy and entertained, and I feel rewarded by seeing only happy, kind faces around me. Since you left, only one change has happened in our small family. Do you remember when Justine Moritz joined us? You probably don’t, so I’ll briefly tell you her story. Madame Moritz, her mother, was a widow with four children, and Justine was the third. This girl was always her father’s favorite, but strangely, her mother couldn’t stand her. After her father died, the mother treated her very poorly. My aunt noticed this and, when Justine was twelve, convinced her mother to let her live with us. The democratic system in our country has created simpler and happier ways of living than the big monarchies around us. Because of this, there is less difference between the different social classes, and the lower classes are not as poor or looked down upon, so their behavior is more refined and moral. A servant in Geneva is not the same as a servant in France and England. Justine, welcomed into our family, learned how to be a servant, a role in our lucky country that does not mean ignorance or loss of human dignity.

You might remember that Justine was a favorite of yours. I remember you once said that if you were in a bad mood, one look from Justine could cheer you up, just like Ariosto said about Angelica’s beauty—she looked so honest and joyful. My aunt really loved Justine and decided to give her a better education than she had planned. Justine was very grateful; I don’t mean she said so, but you could see it in her eyes. She almost worshipped her protector. Even though Justine was cheerful and sometimes careless, she paid close attention to every move my aunt made. She thought my aunt was the perfect example of excellence and tried to copy her words and behavior, so that even now she reminds me of her.

When my dearest aunt died, everyone was too caught up in their own sadness to notice poor Justine, who had taken care of her during her illness with great love. Poor Justine was very sick; but more troubles were waiting for her.

One by one, her brothers and sister died, and her mother, except for her neglected daughter, was left without children. The mother’s conscience was troubled; she began to think that the deaths of her favorite children were a punishment from heaven for her unfair treatment.

“Fiend,” I cried, “do you dare come near me? Do you not fear the terrible wrath of my hand falling upon your wretched skull? Away, foul creature! Or stay, so that I might crush you beneath my feet! And oh, if only I could end your pitiful life and bring back those you have so cruelly taken away!”

“I foresaw this response,” the demon replied. “All men despise the wretched; how much more must I be despised, being the most wretched of all beings! Yet you, my maker, loathe and reject me, your creation, to whom you are bound by ties that can only be broken by the destruction of one of us. You intend to kill me. How dare you toy with life in this way? Fulfill your duty to me, and I shall fulfill mine to you and to mankind. If you agree to my terms, I shall leave you and your kin in peace; but if you refuse, I shall feed the jaws of death until they are sated with the blood of your remaining loved ones.”

“Accursed wretch! Monster that you are! The torments of hell are too lenient for your sins. Miserable demon! You accuse me of your creation—come then, that I may snuff out the spark I so carelessly gave you.”

My fury knew no bounds; I leapt at him, driven by every feeling that could drive one being to destroy another.

He easily avoided me and said,

“Calm yourself! I beg you to listen to me before you unleash your hatred upon my doomed head. Have I not suffered enough, that you would add to my sorrow? Life, though it may be nothing but a collection of sorrows, is precious to me, and I shall defend it. Remember, you have made me stronger than yourself; my height surpasses yours, my joints more flexible. But I will not be lured into opposing you. I am your creation, and I shall be gentle and obedient to my rightful master and king if you, too, fulfill your part, which you owe me. Oh, Frankenstein, do not be just to all others and trample upon me alone, to whom your justice, and even your mercy and affection, are most deserved. Recall that I am your creation; I should be your Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel, whom you drive from joy for no wrongdoing. Everywhere I see happiness, from which I alone am forever excluded. I was kind and good; misery turned me into a monster. Make me happy, and I shall once more be virtuous.”

“Leave me! I will not listen to you. There can be no bond between you and me; we are enemies. Leave, or let us test our strength in a battle, in which one must fall.”

“How can I stir you? Will no pleas cause you to look upon your creature with kindness, who begs for your goodness and compassion? Believe me, Frankenstein, I was kind; my soul burned with love and humanity; but am I not alone, dreadfully alone? You, my creator, despise me; what hope can I have from your fellow men, who owe me nothing? They reject and hate me. The lonely mountains and bleak glaciers are my sanctuary. I have wandered here for many days; the icy caves, which I do not fear, are my home, and the only one which man does not begrudge.

It took me a while to figure out why this kind family was so unhappy. It was poverty, and they were suffering from it badly. They only had vegetables from their garden and milk from one cow for food. The cow barely had enough to eat in the winter, so the family often went hungry, especially the two younger people. I noticed them giving food to the old man while they had nothing left for themselves.

This act of kindness touched me. At night, I had been sneaking some of their food for myself, but when I realized it was hurting them, I stopped. Instead, I ate berries, nuts, and roots I found in the nearby woods.

I also found another way to help. I saw the young man spending a lot of time gathering wood for the fire. At night, I took his tools, learned how to use them, and brought back enough wood for several days.

I remember the first time I did this. In the morning, the young woman opened the door and was surprised to see a big pile of wood outside. She shouted, and the young man joined her, also surprised. I was happy to see he didn’t go to the forest that day but spent time fixing the cottage and working in the garden instead.

Later, I made an even more important discovery. I found out that these people used sounds to share their thoughts and feelings. I noticed that the words they said could bring joy or sadness to others. This was a powerful skill, and I really wanted to learn it. But I struggled because their speech was fast, and the words didn’t clearly connect to things I could see. After a lot of effort and several months in my hovel, I learned the names of some common things like fire, milk, bread, and wood. I also learned the names of the family members. The young man and the girl each had multiple names, but the old man only had one, which was father. The girl was called sister or Agatha, and the young man was Felix, brother, or son. I can’t explain how happy I felt when I learned what these words meant and could say them. I also recognized other words like good, dearest, and unhappy, but I didn’t yet understand how to use them. 

I spent the winter this way. The kind and gentle nature of the family made me care about them deeply. When they were sad, I felt sad too, and when they were happy, I shared in their joy.

Safie told how her mother was a Christian Arab who was captured and enslaved by the Turks. Her beauty caught the attention of Safie's father, and he married her. Safie spoke highly of her mother, who had been born free and refused to accept the slavery she now lived in. Her mother taught her about her religion and encouraged her to seek knowledge and independence, which Muslim women were not allowed. Her mother died, but her teachings stayed with Safie. She was unhappy at the thought of returning to Asia and being locked up in a harem, where she would be forced to do childish things that didn't suit her strong and noble spirit. She was happy at the idea of marrying a Christian and staying in a place where women had a place in society.

The day the Turk was to be executed was set, but the night before he left his prison and by morning was far away from Paris. Felix had gotten fake passports in the names of his father, sister, and himself. He had already told the Turk about his plan, and the Turk helped by pretending to go on a trip and hiding with his daughter in a quiet part of Paris.

Felix led the runaways through France to Lyons and over Mont Cenis to Leghorn, where the merchant planned to wait for a good chance to go to some part of the Turkish lands.

Safie decided to stay with her father until he left. Before he went, the Turk promised again that she would marry her rescuer. Felix stayed with them, hoping for that to happen. In the meantime, he enjoyed being with Safie, who showed him simple and warm affection. They talked through an interpreter or sometimes just by looking at each other, and Safie sang to him the beautiful songs of her homeland.

The Turk allowed this friendship and encouraged the young lovers' hopes, even though he had other plans in mind. He hated the idea of his daughter marrying a Christian, but he feared Felix's anger if he seemed uninterested. He knew Felix could still turn him in to the Italian government. The Turk thought of many ways to keep the deception going until it was no longer needed, and to secretly take his daughter with him when he left. His plans were helped by news from Paris.

The French government was very angry about the Turk's escape and worked hard to find and punish his rescuer. Felix's plan was quickly discovered, and De Lacey and Agatha were put in prison. The news reached Felix and woke him from his happy dreams. His blind, old father and gentle sister were in a dirty prison while he enjoyed the fresh air and the company of the woman he loved.

The poor who came to their door were never turned away. I admit, I asked for more than just a little food or a place to rest—I wanted kindness and sympathy. I didn’t think I was completely unworthy of it.

The winter had advanced, and a full cycle of the seasons had passed since I came to life. At this point, my focus was entirely on how to introduce myself to the people in the cottage who had helped me. I considered many plans, but the one I finally settled on was to enter the house when the blind old man was alone. I was smart enough to realize that the unnatural ugliness of my appearance was what scared people most when they saw me before. My voice, though rough, wasn’t really frightening, so I thought that if I could win over the old De Lacey while his kids were away, he might help me gain acceptance from the younger ones.

One day, the sun shone on the red leaves scattered on the ground, bringing a bit of cheerfulness even though it didn’t offer much warmth. Safie, Agatha, and Felix went for a long walk in the countryside, and the old man, as he had asked, stayed alone in the cottage. After his kids left, he picked up his guitar and played several sad but sweet tunes, sadder and sweeter than I had ever heard him play before. At first, his face showed pleasure, but as he played on, his expression turned thoughtful and sad. Eventually, he put the instrument aside and sat lost in thought.

My heart raced. This was the moment of truth, the time that would either bring my hopes to life or confirm my fears. The servants had gone to a nearby fair. Everything was quiet in and around the cottage—it was the perfect chance. Yet, when I tried to carry out my plan, my legs gave out and I collapsed to the ground. I got up again, mustering all the strength I could, and removed the planks I had placed in front of my hovel to hide my hiding place. The fresh air revived me, and with renewed determination, I walked toward the door of their cottage.

I knocked. 'Who is it?' the old man asked. 'Come in.'

I stepped inside. 'Sorry to bother you,' I said. 'I'm a traveler in need of a little rest. I'd really appreciate it if you'd let me sit by the fire for a few minutes.'

'Come in,' De Lacey said. 'I'll do what I can to help you out, but unfortunately, my kids are out, and since I'm blind, I'm afraid I'll have a hard time getting you anything to eat.'

'Don't trouble yourself, kind sir,' I replied. 'I've got food. All I need is warmth and a bit of rest.'

I sat down, and a silence followed. I knew every minute was precious, but I still couldn't decide how to start the conversation when the old man finally spoke.

'By your accent, stranger, I'd guess you're from my country. Are you French?'

'No,' I said. 'I was raised by a French family and only speak that language. I'm heading to some friends I truly care about and hope they'll welcome me.'

I spent the rest of the day in my hovel in complete and hopeless despair. My protectors had left, and they had broken the only connection I had to the world. For the first time, feelings of revenge and hatred filled my heart, and I didn't try to control them. I let myself be carried away by these emotions, focusing my thoughts on harm and death. When I thought of my friends, the kind voice of De Lacey, the gentle eyes of Agatha, and the beauty of the Arabian girl, these thoughts disappeared for a moment, and I cried a bit, which gave me some comfort. But when I remembered that they had rejected and abandoned me, anger returned, a strong and fierce anger. Since I couldn't hurt anyone, I turned my anger toward objects. As night grew, I gathered different flammable materials around the cottage and destroyed all signs of cultivation in the garden. I waited impatiently until the moon had set before I began my plan.

"As the night went on, a strong wind rose from the woods and quickly scattered the clouds that had lingered in the sky. The wind blew like a huge avalanche and made me feel wild and out of control. I lit a dry branch of a tree and danced around the cottage with fury, my eyes fixed on the western horizon where the moon was almost touching. Part of the moon disappeared, and I waved my burning branch. It sank, and with a loud scream, I set fire to the straw, heath, and bushes I had gathered. The wind helped the fire spread, and the cottage was soon surrounded by flames, which clung to it and licked it with their forked and destructive tongues.

"As soon as I was sure that no help could save any part of the house, I left the scene and found shelter in the woods.

"Now, with the world before me, where should I go? I decided to run far from the place of my misfortunes; but to me, hated and despised, every country would be equally terrible. Eventually, the thought of you came to my mind. I learned from your papers that you were my father, my creator; and who else could I turn to but the one who had given me life? Among the lessons that Felix had given Safie, geography had not been left out; I had learned from these the positions of the different countries on the earth. You had mentioned Geneva as the name of your hometown, and toward this place I decided to go.

"But how was I to find my way? I knew I had to travel in a southwesterly direction to reach my destination, but the sun was my only guide. I didn't know the names of the towns I would pass through, nor could I ask for help from anyone. But I didn't give up. Only from you could I hope for help, although I felt nothing but hatred toward you. Unfeeling, heartless creator! You gave me senses and emotions and then left me out in the world to be the object of human scorn and fear.

The crime started with her—let her face the consequences! Thanks to Felix's teachings and the brutal laws of society, I had learned how to cause trouble. I leaned over her and carefully tucked the portrait into one of the folds of her dress. She moved again, and I ran away.

For a few days, I kept returning to the place where these events happened, sometimes hoping to see you, sometimes determined to leave the world and its pain behind forever. Eventually, I headed toward these mountains and wandered through their vast, empty spaces, driven by a burning passion only you can satisfy. We won't part ways until you promise to meet my demand. I'm alone and miserable; no one wants to be around me. But someone as deformed and terrible as I am wouldn't turn me away. My partner must be from the same species and share my flaws. You're the only one who can create this being for me.'

The creature finished speaking and stared at me, waiting for my response. But I was confused, overwhelmed, and couldn't think clearly enough to grasp the full weight of his request. He went on,

'You must create a female for me, someone I can live with and share the feelings I need to survive. Only you can do this, and I'm demanding it as a right you can't deny me.'

The second part of his story reignited the anger I had forgotten while he described his peaceful life with the cottagers, and when he said this, I could no longer hold back the rage inside me.

'I refuse,' I said. 'No amount of pain will ever make me agree. You can make me the saddest person alive, but you'll never make me feel ashamed. Would you really create another like yourself, whose combined evil could destroy the world? Leave me alone! I've answered you; you can hurt me all you want, but I'll never say yes.'

'You're wrong,' the creature replied. 'Instead of threatening me, I'm willing to talk things out with you. I'm cruel because I'm unhappy. Don't I get shunned and hated by everyone? You, my creator, would tear me apart and feel victorious. Remember that, and tell me why I should care about humans more than they care about me? You wouldn't call it murder if you threw me into one of those ice cracks and ended my life, which you made. Should I respect people who condemn me? Let them live with me in kindness, and I'd give them everything I could with tears of gratitude for accepting me. But that's impossible; human nature is an unbreakable wall between us. Still, I won't accept the submission of a slave. I'll take revenge for my suffering; if I can't inspire love, I'll inspire fear, especially toward you, my worst enemy, because you're my creator. I swear I'll never stop hating you. Be careful; I'll destroy you, and I won't stop until your heart is broken and you curse the day you were born.'

A furious anger showed in his face as he said this; his expression twisted into something too awful to look at. But soon he calmed down and continued,

'I meant to reason.'

Things had definitely changed for me. My health, which had been getting worse, was now much better, and my mood, when I wasn't weighed down by the memory of my unhappy promise, had lifted right along with it. My father noticed this and was pleased. He started thinking about the best way to get rid of the last traces of my sadness, which would sometimes come back in waves, dark and all-consuming, even when the sun was about to shine again. During those times, I would retreat into complete solitude. I would spend entire days alone on the lake in a small boat, watching the clouds and listening to the gentle lapping of the waves, feeling quiet and unmotivated. But the fresh air and bright sun usually helped me feel calmer, and when I came back, I greeted my friends with a more cheerful smile and a lighter heart.

It was after one of these outings that my father pulled me aside and spoke to me like this:

“I’m glad to see, my dear son, that you’ve started enjoying the things you used to again and seem to be getting back to your old self. And yet, you still seem unhappy and avoid our company. For a while, I wasn’t sure why, but yesterday it hit me. If I’m right, I urge you to tell me. Keeping things to yourself on this issue would not only be pointless, but it would bring even more misery to all of us.”

I shook badly at the start of his speech, and he went on:

“I’ll admit, my son, that I’ve always imagined your marriage to our dear Elizabeth as the foundation of our family’s happiness and the support of my old age. You two have been close since childhood; you studied together and seemed perfectly matched in personality and interests. But human experience is so limited that what I thought would help bring things together might have actually torn it apart. Perhaps you see her as your sister, with no desire for her to become your wife. Or maybe you’ve met someone else you love, and the pressure of feeling honor-bound to Elizabeth is causing the deep pain you seem to be going through.”

“My dear father, don’t worry. I love my cousin deeply and genuinely. I’ve never met a woman who inspires in me the kind of admiration and affection Elizabeth does. My future hopes and dreams are all tied to the idea of us being together.”

“Hearing you speak like this, my dear Victor, brings me more joy than I’ve felt in a while. If you feel that way, we’ll surely be happy, even if current events cast a shadow over us. We’ve had bad luck, and recent events have disrupted the peace I need for my age and health. You’re younger, but I don’t think, with the fortune you have, that getting married early would interfere with any future plans you might have for honor and usefulness.”

I thought I could land almost anywhere, but I couldn’t—the bank was too steep. I got to the bottom of the island before I found a good spot. I went into the woods and decided I wouldn’t fool around with rafts anymore, as long as they kept moving the lantern around. I had my pipe, some tobacco, and matches in my cap, and they weren’t wet, so I was all set.

“And you haven’t had any meat or bread to eat all this time? Why didn’t you get mud-turtles?”

“How would you catch them? You can’t sneak up on them and grab them, and how would you hit them with a rock? How could you do it at night? And I wasn’t going to show myself on the bank during the day.”

“Well, that’s true. You had to stay in the woods all the time, of course. Did you hear them shooting the cannon?”

“Oh, yes. I knew they were after you. I saw them go by here—watched them through the bushes.

And Jim said you shouldn’t count the things you are going to cook for dinner, because that would bring bad luck. The same if you shook the tablecloth after sunset. And he said if a man owned a beehive and that man died, the bees must be told about it before sunrise the next morning, or else the bees would weaken and stop working and die. I had heard about some of these things before, but not all of them. Jim knew all kinds of signs. He said he knew most everything. I said it looked to me like all the signs were about bad luck, and so I asked him if there weren’t any good-luck signs. He said:

“Very few—and they aren’t any use to a person. What would you want to know when good luck’s coming for? “What’s the use of asking that question? Don’t you see I do?”

“Well, are you rich?”

“No, but I was rich once, and I’m going to be rich again.”

Every night now, I used to sneak onto land around ten o'clock at some small town and buy ten to fifteen cents worth of flour, bacon, or other food to eat. Sometimes I'd grab a chicken that wasn't roosting comfortably and take it with me. Pap always said to take a chicken when you had the chance because if you didn't want it yourself, you could always find someone who did, and doing a good deed was never forgotten. I never saw Pap when he didn't want the chicken himself, but that's what he used to say anyway.

In the mornings before daylight, I'd sneak into cornfields and borrow a watermelon, a mushmelon, a pumpkin, or some fresh corn or similar stuff. Pap always said it wasn't wrong to borrow things if you planned to pay them back eventually; but the widow said it was just a fancy name for stealing, and no decent person would do it. Jim said he thought the widow was partly right and Pap was partly right; so the best way would be for us to pick out two or three things from the list and decide not to borrow them anymore—then he figured it wouldn't be wrong to borrow the others. So we talked it over one night, drifting down the river, trying to decide whether to give up watermelons, cantaloupes, mushmelons, or something else. But by daylight we had it all settled and decided to drop crabapples and persimmons. We hadn't felt right before that, but now everything was comfortable. I was glad the way it turned out too, because crabapples are never good, and persimmons wouldn't be ripe for two or three months yet.

We shot a waterfowl now and then that got up too early in the morning or stayed out too late at night. All things considered, we lived pretty well.

After a while, I said, 'Hey, Jim, look over there!' It was a steamboat that had crashed into a rock. We were drifting straight toward it. The lightning showed it clearly. It was leaning over, with part of its upper deck above water, and you could see every little chimney guy clean and clear, and a chair by the big bell, with an old slouch hat hanging on the back of it when the flashes came.

Well, it being late at night and stormy, and everything so mysterious, I felt just the way any other kid would have felt when I saw that wreck lying there so sad and lonely in the middle of the river. I wanted to get aboard and sneak around a bit, to see what was there. So I said:

“I am, am I? Well, you answer me this: Didn’t you bring out the line in the canoe to get to the tow-head?”

“No, I didn’t. What tow-head? I haven’t seen any tow-head.”

“You haven’t seen a tow-head? Look here, didn’t the line come loose and the raft start heading down the river, leaving you and the canoe behind in the fog?”

“What fog?”

“Well, the fog—the fog that’s been around all night. And didn’t you yell, and didn’t I yell, until we got mixed up in the islands and one of us got lost and the other was just as good as lost, because he didn’t know where he was? And didn’t I crash into a bunch of those islands and have a terrible time and almost drown? Now isn’t that true, boss—isn’t it true? You answer me that.”

“Well, then, I reckon I did dream it, Huck; but dog my cats if it ain’t the strongest dream I ever had. And I haven’t ever had no dream before that’s tired me like this one.”

“Oh, well, that’s all right, because a dream does tire a body like everything sometimes. But this one was a stunner; tell me all about it, Jim.”

So Jim started in and told me the whole thing through, just as it happened, only he added a lot of extra details. Then he said he had to start interpreting it, because it was sent as a warning. He said the first tow-head stood for a man that would try to do us some good, but the current was another man that would get us away from him. The yells were warnings that would come to us every now and then, and if we didn’t try hard to understand them, they’d just lead us into bad luck instead of keeping us out of it. The bunch of tow-heads was trouble we were going to get into with quarrelsome people and all kinds of mean folks, but if we minded our business and didn’t argue back and aggravate them, we would pull through and get out of the fog and into the big clear river, which was the free States, and wouldn’t have no more trouble.

It had gotten pretty dark just after I got on the raft, but it was clearing up again now.

“Oh, well, that’s all interpreted well enough as far as it goes, Jim,” I said; “but what do these things stand for?”

The residents had already left some of them. The bank had collapsed under one corner of others, and that corner was about to fall in. People still lived in those houses, but it was risky, because sometimes a strip of land as wide as a house would collapse at once. Sometimes a stretch of land a quarter-mile deep would begin to cave in and keep going until it all tumbled into the river in a single summer. A town like that had to keep moving back and back and back, because the river was always wearing it away.

The closer it got to noon that day, the more wagons and horses filled the streets, and more kept coming all the time. Country folks brought their lunches and ate them in the wagons. There was a fair amount of drinking going on, and I saw three fights. Then someone shouted out:

“Here comes old Boggs!—he’s in town for his monthly little spree; here he comes, boys!”

All the idlers looked pleased; I figured they were used to getting amusement from Boggs. One of them said:

“Wonder who he’s going to chew out this time. If he’d chewed out all the men he’s been going to chew out in the last twenty years, he’d have quite a reputation now.”

Another one said, “I wish old Boggs would threaten me, ’cause then I’d know I wasn’t going to die for a thousand years.”

Boggs came tearing along on his horse, whooping and yelling like an Indian, and shouting:

“Clear the track, there. I’m on the war-path, and the price of coffins is going to rise.”

He was drunk and swaying in his saddle; he was over fifty years old, and had a very red face. Everyone yelled at him and laughed at him and teased him, and he teased back, and said he’d take care of them and lay them out in their turn, but he couldn’t wait now because he’d come to town to kill old Colonel Sherburn, and his motto was, “Meat first, and spoon vittles to top off on.”

He saw me, and rode up and said:

“Where’d you come from, boy? You ready to die?”

Then he rode on. I was scared, but a man said:

“He don’t mean nothing; he’s always carrying on like that when he’s drunk. He’s the best-natured old fool in Arkansas—never hurt nobody, drunk or sober.”

Boggs rode up in front of the biggest store in town, and bent his head down so he could see under the curtain of the awning and yelled:

“Come out here, Sherburn! Come out and meet the man you’ve swindled. You’re the hound I’m after, and I’m going to get you, too!”

He said to Boggs, very calm and slow—he said:

“I’m tired of this, but I’ll put up with it till one o’clock.”

He kept walking around, talking a lot and enjoying the sound of his own voice. Every now and then, he brought up the topic of funeral ceremonies again. Eventually, the duke couldn’t take it anymore. He wrote on a small piece of paper, ‘_obsequies_, you old fool,’ folded it up, and passed it over people’s heads to him. The king read it, put it in his pocket, and said:

“Poor William, who is troubled, has a good heart. He asked me to invite everyone to the funeral and to make them all feel welcome. But he didn’t need to worry—it was exactly what I was going to do anyway.”

Then he continued walking calmly, bringing up the funeral ceremonies again every now and then, just like before. When he did it the third time, he said:

“I say ‘orgies’ not because it’s the common term—it isn’t; ‘obsequies’ is the common term—but because ‘orgies’ is the right term. ‘Obsequies’ isn’t used in England anymore—it’s out of style. We say ‘orgies’ now in England. ‘Orgies’ is better because it means the thing you’re after more exactly. It’s a word made up from the Greek _orgo_, meaning outside, open, or abroad, and the Hebrew _jeesum_, meaning to plant or cover up; hence, in_ter_. So you see, funeral orgies is an open or public funeral.”

He was the worst I ever met. The iron-jawed man laughed right in his face. Everyone was shocked. They all said, “Why, doctor!” and Abner Shackleford said:

“Why, Robinson, haven’t you heard the news? This is Harvey Wilks.”

The king smiled eagerly, reached out his hand, and said:

“Is it my poor brother’s dear good friend and physician? I—”

“Keep your hands off of me!” said the doctor. “Do you think you sound like an Englishman? It’s the worst imitation I’ve ever heard. Are you Peter Wilks’s brother? You’re a fraud, that’s what you are!”

Well, how they all reacted! They crowded around the doctor, trying to calm him down and explain how Harvey had shown in forty ways that he really was Harvey, knew everyone by name, even the names of the dogs, and begged and begged him not to hurt Harvey’s feelings or the poor girl’s feelings. But it didn’t help; he kept yelling, saying any man who pretended to be an Englishman and couldn’t imitate the language better than that was a fraud and a liar. The poor girls were holding onto the king and crying; and all of a sudden, the doctor turned on them. He said:

“I was your father’s friend, and I’m your friend. I warn you as a friend, and an honest one who wants to protect you and keep you out of harm and trouble, to turn your backs on that scoundrel and have nothing to do with him, the ignorant tramp, with his idiotic Greek and Hebrew, as he calls it. He is the thinnest kind of an impostor—he came here with a lot of empty names and facts which he picked up somewhere, and you take them for proofs, and are helped to fool yourselves by these foolish friends here, who ought to know better.”

They are always easy to find. There is nothing at all mysterious about them. They take carriage rides in the park in the morning and talk endlessly at tea gatherings in the afternoon. They wear the same polished smile and display the same fashionable manner. They are completely predictable. But an actress! How entirely different an actress is! Harry, why didn’t you tell me that the only thing truly worth loving is an actress?”

He stood up and looked out the window. The sunset had turned the windows of the houses across the street a deep red gold. The glass looked like hot metal. The sky above was the color of a faded rose. He thought about his friend’s young, passionate life and wondered how it would all end.

When he got home, around half past twelve, he saw a telegram on the hall table. He opened it and saw it was from Dorian Gray. It said he was going to be married to Sibyl Vane.


CHAPTER V.


“Mother, Mother, I’m so happy!” the girl whispered, hiding her face in the lap of the older, tired-looking woman who sat in the only armchair in their small, shabby room. “I’m so happy!” she said again. “And you must be happy too!”

Mrs. Vane winced and placed her pale, white-powdered hands on her daughter’s head. “Happy?” she repeated. “I’m only happy when I see you act. You must think only about your acting. Mr. Isaacs has been very kind to us, and we owe him money.”

The girl looked up and pouted. “Money, Mother?” she said. “What does money matter? Love is more than money.”

“Mr. Isaacs gave us fifty pounds to pay our debts and to get a proper outfit for James. You must not forget that, Sibyl. Fifty pounds is a lot. Mr. Isaacs has been very generous.”

“He isn’t a gentleman, Mother, and I hate the way he talks to me,” the girl said, standing up and walking to the window.

“I don’t know how we could manage without him,” the older woman replied, sounding upset.

Sibyl Vane shook her head and laughed. “We don’t need him anymore, Mother. Prince Charming is in charge of our lives now.” Then she stopped. A rose bloomed in her cheeks. Her breath came quickly, like petals parting. Her lips trembled. A warm wind of passion moved through her and lifted the soft folds of her dress. “I love him,” she said simply.

“Foolish child! Foolish child!” the mother said, repeating the words. Her thin fingers, decorated with fake jewels, waved in the air, making the words seem silly.

The girl laughed again. Her voice sounded like the joy of a bird in a cage. Her eyes caught the sound and reflected it in light, then closed for a moment as if to hide something. When they opened, a dream had passed over them.

From the worn chair came a voice, thin and full of caution, offering advice and quoting the book of common sense. She didn’t listen. She felt free in her prison of passion. Her prince, Prince Charming, was with her. She had asked memory to bring him back. She had sent her soul to find him, and it had returned with him. His kiss burned again on her lips. Her eyelids were warm with his breath.

Then the voice changed and spoke of secrets and being discovered. This young man might be rich. If so, marriage should be considered. Against the side of her ear came the waves of worldly cleverness.

He was supposed to get off the ship in Melbourne, say a polite goodbye to the captain, and head straight to the goldfields. Within a week, he was going to discover a huge chunk of pure gold, the biggest ever found, and bring it down to the coast in a wagon guarded by six armed police on horseback. The bushrangers were going to attack them three times and be badly beaten each time. Or, no. He wasn’t going to go to the goldfields at all. They were terrible places where men got drunk, shot each other in bars, and used bad language. He was supposed to be a nice sheep farmer, and one evening, while riding home, he would see the beautiful heiress being kidnapped by a robber on a black horse, chase after her, and rescue her. Of course, she would fall in love with him, and he with her, and they would get married and live in a huge house in London. Yes, there were great things in store for him. But he had to be really good, not lose his temper, or spend his money foolishly. She was only a year older than him, but she knew so much more about life. He also had to make sure to write to her with every mail and say his prayers each night before going to sleep. God was really good and would look out for him. She would pray for him too, and in a few years he would come back rich and happy.

The boy listened sulkily and didn’t say a word. He was heartbroken about leaving home.

But it wasn’t just that which made him gloomy and moody. Even though he was inexperienced, he had a strong sense of the danger Sibyl was in. This young guy who was flirting with her wasn’t going to do her any good. He was a gentleman, and he hated him for that, hated him for some strange instinct he couldn’t explain, and because of that, it was even stronger inside him. He also realized how shallow and vain his mother was, and in that, he saw a huge threat to Sibyl and her happiness. Kids start by loving their parents; as they get older, they judge them; sometimes they forgive them.

His mother! He had something on his mind he wanted to ask her, something he had been thinking about for months of silence. A random comment he had overheard at the theater, a whispered sneer that had reached his ears one night while he was waiting at the stage door, had triggered a series of terrible thoughts. He remembered it as if it had been a whip across his face. His eyebrows furrowed into a deep frown, and with a twitch of pain, he bit his lower lip.

He shrugged. “You’re more likely to forget me than I am to forget you, Sibyl.”

“That’s absolutely true, Dorian,” cried Hallward.

“Nothing is ever absolutely true,” said Lord Henry.

“This is,” interrupted Dorian. “You have to admit, Harry, that women give men the very best of themselves.”

“Possibly,” he sighed, “but they always want it back in tiny pieces. That’s the problem. Women, as some clever Frenchman once said, inspire us with the desire to do masterpieces and always stop us from doing them.”

“Harry, you’re terrible! I don’t know why I like you so much.”

“Pleasure is the only thing worth having a theory about,” he answered in his slow, musical voice. “But I’m afraid I can’t say it’s my own idea. It belongs to Nature, not me. Pleasure is Nature’s test, her sign of approval. When we are happy, we are always good, but when we are good, we are not always happy.”

“Ah! But what do you mean by good?” cried Basil Hallward.

“Yes,” echoed Dorian, leaning back in his chair and looking at Lord Henry over the heavy clusters of purple-lipped irises that stood in the center of the table, “what do you mean by good, Harry?”

“To be good is to be in harmony with oneself,” he replied, touching the thin stem of his glass with his pale, fine-pointed fingers. “Discord is being forced to be in harmony with others. One’s own life—that is the important thing. As for the lives of one’s neighbors, if one wants to be a prig or a Puritan, one can flaunt one’s moral views about them, but they are not one’s concern. Besides, individualism has the higher aim. Modern morality consists in accepting the standard of one’s age. I consider that for any man of culture to accept the standard of his age is a form of the grossest immorality.”

“But, surely, if one lives merely for oneself, Harry, one pays a terrible price for doing so?” suggested the painter.

“Yes, we are overcharged for everything nowadays. I should think that the real tragedy of the poor is that they can afford nothing but self-denial. Beautiful sins, like beautiful things, are the privilege of the rich.”

“One has to pay in other ways but money.”

“What sort of ways, Basil?”

“Oh! I should think in remorse, in suffering, in ... well, in the consciousness of degradation.”

Lord Henry shrugged his shoulders. “My dear fellow, medieval art is charming, but medieval emotions are out of date. One can use them in fiction, of course. But then the only things one can use in fiction are the things one has stopped using in real life. Believe me, no civilized man ever regrets a pleasure, and no uncivilized man ever knows what a pleasure is.”

“I know what pleasure is,” cried Dorian Gray. “It is to adore someone.”

“That is certainly better than being adored,” he answered, toying with some fruits. “Being adored is a nuisance. Women treat us just as humanity treats its gods. They worship us, and are always bothering us to do something for them.”

“I should have said that whatever they ask for they had first given to us,” murmured the lad seriously. “They create love in our natures. They have a right to demand it back.”

“That is quite true, Dorian,” cried Hallward.

“Nothing is ever quite true,” said Lord Henry.

“This is,” interrupted Dorian. “You must admit, Harry, that women give to men the very gold of their lives.”

“Possibly,” he sighed, “but they always want it back in such small change. That is the worry. Women, as some witty Frenchman once put it, inspire us with the desire to do masterpieces and always prevent us from carrying them out.”

“Harry, you are dreadful! I don’t know why I like you so much.”

And yet, the thing would still live on. It would always be alive.

He shivered, and for a moment he wished he had told Basil the real reason he wanted to hide the painting. Basil would have helped him resist Lord Henry's influence and the even worse influence from his own nature. The love he felt for Basil—because it really was love—was noble and intellectual. It wasn't just a physical admiration of beauty that comes from the senses and fades when the senses get tired. It was the kind of love Michelangelo, Montaigne, Winckelmann, and Shakespeare himself had known. Yes, Basil could have saved him. But now it was too late. The past could always be erased. Regret, denial, or forgetfulness could do that. But the future was unavoidable. There were passions in him that would find their terrible release, and dreams that would make the shadow of their evil real.

He picked up the large purple-and-gold fabric that covered the couch and, holding it in his hands, went behind the screen. Was the face on the canvas worse than before? It seemed unchanged to him, and yet his hatred of it had grown. Golden hair, blue eyes, and rose-red lips—they were all still there. It was just the expression that had changed. That was cruel and horrifying. Compared to what he saw in it of blame or criticism, how shallow Basil's complaints about Sibyl Vane had been!—how shallow, and how unimportant! His own soul was looking out at him from the canvas and calling him to judgment. A look of pain crossed his face, and he threw the rich cloth over the painting. As he did, a knock came at the door. He left the room just as his servant entered.

“The men are here, Monsieur.”

He felt the man had to be sent away right away. He couldn't be allowed to know where the painting was being taken. There was something sneaky about him, and he had thoughtful, treacherous eyes. Sitting at the writing desk, he quickly wrote a note to Lord Henry, asking him to send something to read and reminding him they were to meet at eight-fifteen that evening.

“Wait for an answer,” he said, handing it to the servant, “and show the men in here.”

In two or three minutes, there was another knock, and Mr. Hubbard himself, the famous frame-maker from South Audley Street, came in with a somewhat rough-looking young assistant. Mr. Hubbard was a red-faced, red-whiskered little man whose love for art was often mixed with the constant financial struggles of most of the artists who dealt with him. Usually, he never left his shop. He waited for people to come to him. But he always made an exception for Dorian Gray. There was something about Dorian that charmed everyone. It was a pleasure even to see him.

“What can I do for you, Mr. Gray?” he asked, rubbing his fat, freckled hands. “I thought I'd do myself the honor of coming round in person. I just got a beautiful frame, sir. Found it at a sale.”

Even reading about the luxury of the dead was amazing.

Then he focused on embroidery and tapestries, which served as wall decorations in the cold rooms of northern European countries. As he studied the topic—something he always had a knack for getting totally absorbed in—he felt a bit sad about how time ruined beautiful and amazing things. At least he had avoided that. Summer after summer passed, the yellow jonquils bloomed and died many times, and nights of horror repeated their shameful stories, but he remained the same. No winter aged his face or dulled his youthful glow. How different it was for physical objects! Where had they gone? Where was the big crocus-colored robe, where gods battled giants, made by brown-skinned girls for Athena’s pleasure? Where was the massive purple awning Nero had hung over the Colosseum in Rome, that huge sail-like piece showing the starry sky and Apollo driving a chariot pulled by golden-reined white horses? He wanted to see the strange tablecloths made for the Priest of the Sun, which showed all the delicacies needed for a feast; the funeral cloth of King Chilperic, covered in 300 golden bees; the wild robes that upset the Bishop of Pontus and were decorated with lions, panthers, bears, dogs, forests, rocks, hunters—basically everything a painter could copy from nature; and the coat Charles of Orleans once wore, with the sleeves embroidered with the lyrics of a song starting with 'Madame, je suis tout joyeux,' the musical notes in gold thread, each square note made with four pearls. He read about the room set up in the palace at Rheims for Queen Joan of Burgundy, decorated with 1321 embroidered parrots showing the king’s crest and 561 butterflies with the queen’s crest on their wings, all in gold. Catherine de Medici had a black velvet mourning bed covered in crescents and suns. Its curtains were damask with leafy wreaths and garlands on a gold and silver background, with pearl-embroidered edges, and it was in a room lined with rows of the queen’s symbols in black velvet on silver cloth. Louis XIV had fifteen-foot-tall gold-embroidered caryatides in his room. The state bed of Sobieski, King of Poland, was made of Smyrna gold brocade embroidered with turquoise verses from the Koran. Its supports were gold-plated silver, beautifully carved and covered with enamel and jeweled medallions. It had been taken from the Turkish camp before Vienna, and the flag of Mohammed had flown under its shimmering gold canopy.

And so, for a whole year, he tried to collect the most exquisite examples of textile and embroidery work he could find, including the delicate Delhi muslins, finely decorated with gold-thread palm designs and stitched with iridescent beetle wings; the Dacca gauzes, known in the East as 'woven air,' 'running water,' and 'evening dew'; strange patterned fabrics from Java; detailed yellow Chinese hangings; books bound in tawny satins or blue silks and decorated with lilies, birds, and images; veils of lace made in Hungary; Sicilian brocades and stiff Spanish velvets; Georgian work with gold coins, and Japanese Foukousas with their green-toned golds and beautifully feathered birds.

There was a terrible allure to them all. He saw them at night, and they haunted his thoughts in the day. The Renaissance was familiar with peculiar methods of poisoning—poisoning by a helmet and a lit torch, by an embroidered glove and a jeweled fan, by a gilded pomander and an amber chain. Dorian Gray had been poisoned by a book. There were times when he regarded evil merely as a means through which he could express his vision of beauty.

CHAPTER XII.

It was on the ninth of November, the night before his thirty-eighth birthday, as he often recalled later.

He was returning home about eleven o’clock from Lord Henry’s, where he had dined, and was wrapped in thick furs, as the night was cold and foggy. At the corner of Grosvenor Square and South Audley Street, a man passed him in the mist, walking swiftly with the collar of his grey ulster turned up. He had a bag in his hand. Dorian recognized him. It was Basil Hallward. A peculiar sense of dread, for which he could not explain, overtook him. He gave no sign of recognition and hurried on toward his own home.

But Hallward had noticed him. Dorian heard him first pause on the pavement and then rush after him. In a few moments, his hand was on his arm.

“Dorian! What an extraordinary coincidence! I’ve been waiting for you in your library since nine o’clock. Eventually, I took pity on your exhausted servant and told him to go to bed, as he let me out.”
